item.title: The AI Hype Index: AI is everywhere
item.dc:creator: Amit Katwala
item.description: Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and…
item.content:encoded:
Like a nasty rash, AI seems to spread everywhere. Google crams AI Overviews down your throat even though it costs the company billions of dollars in lost ad revenue. Leave your apartment, and you might pass two people heaving an AI-powered humanoid robot up the stairs to clean someone’s rooms. Go to the supermarket, and perhaps you’ll slip on a pool of melted ice cream congealing on the floor thanks to an AI-assisted cyberattack. 

You go to the movies and see Sam Altman being played with nauseating intensity by Andrew Garfield, and go back home to find that Elon Musk has released a Grok-fied version of The Odyssey. You try to watch it, but it feels like a long, unskippable mobile ad. In a way, the whole world kind of feels that way now: Like a modern Odysseus, you are cursed to roam AI-infested waters, dueling with machine gods and monsters, trying to find your way back to somewhere that feels like home.

item.title: The Download: AI learns to smell and hydropower struggles
item.dc:creator: Thomas Macaulay
item.description: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. item.content:encoded:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s

In a New Jersey lab, researchers are trying to sniff every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with chemical analyses to train what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. Its goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

Wiltschko claims the model has already achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence” and is helping fragrance brands design new scents. But Osmo has bigger ambitions, from detecting counterfeit goods to diagnosing diseases. Not everyone is convinced its technology can deliver.

How far could an AI-powered sense of smell really take us?

—Amit Katwala

Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer

The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. But an extreme, prolonged drought has left water levels dangerously low in the region’s two largest reservoirs—and climate change is adding to the pressure.

Find out how climate change is threatening a vital source of renewable power.

—Casey Crownhart

MIT Technology Review Narrated: How solid-state transformers could help power the AI boom

Transformers are a crucial but nearly invisible part of the US grid, helping move power efficiently across long distances. But they’re complicated and in short supply, and their basic design hasn’t changed much in about a century.

As electricity demand rises from EVs, data centers, and more, plans are emerging to modernize these grid staples. Solid-state versions could help ease supply concerns and cut power losses. The technology is still in development, but it could become a crucial part of our future grid.

This is our latest story to become an MIT Technology Review Narrated podcast, which we publish each week on Spotify and Apple Podcasts. Just navigate to MIT Technology Review Narrated on either platform, and follow us to get all our new content as it’s released.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 The wave of outages has reached the US government and Apple
The agency’s classified communications network has gone down. (CNN)
+ An update disrupted Apple Music, App Store, and AppleCare. (AP)
+ The issues join a recent flood of outages at critical services. (CNBC)
+ Marco Rubio says they’re unrelated and not hostile acts. (Guardian)
+ But AI is accelerating the discovery of vulnerabilities. (Vox)
+ And making online crimes easier. (MIT Technology Review)

2 Measles is officially endemic again in the US
Scientists blame persistent gaps in vaccination coverage. (Guardian)
+ This year’s outbreak is the deadliest since 1991. (Nature)
+ Mexico and Bolivia also lost their measles elimination status. (DW)
+ Other infections could be next. (MIT Technology Review)

3 Only nine countries have backed COP31’s AI climate pledge
The voluntary pledge doesn’t include binding targets. (Reuters $)
+ Plans for carbon removal tech have divided COP31. (New Scientist $)
+ For all its flaws, the annual climate meeting still matters. (Axios)
+ What to know about this year’s talks. (MIT Technology Review)

4 Nvidia has delivered blowout results and rejected Huang’s return
Revenue more than doubled amid booming AI chip sales. (Axios)
+ Nvidia has stopped shipments of H200 chips to China. (Gizmodo)
+ China has threatened countermeasures over new chip curbs. (Reuters $)

5 More than a third of Gen-Z relies on AI for friendship
Those who do have higher odds of loneliness. (Wired $)

6 Ukraine says Starshield speed limits remain in occupied territory
Zelenskyy said the restrictions hamper air defences. (CNBC)

7 San Diego has dumped Flock cameras and smart streetlights
It’s shutting down more than 500 surveillance cameras. (Ars Technica)
+ What Flock’s defenders are missing. (MIT Technology Review)

8 Waymo has pulled its driverless taxis from US freeways
The move comes after California banned freeway trips. (NBC News)

9 Lakes are becoming strangely synchronized
Scientists warn this could lead to ecological collapses. (404 Media)

10 “Human” has won the Cambridge Dictionary’s word of the year
The dictionary says the word has gained importance in the AI age. (BBC)

Quote of the day

“It’s life. When you’re big and powerful and you have all the money, things like that happen. It’s fine.”

—Donald Trump shrugs off a week of outages that grounded flights, locked customers out of their banks, and knocked out an NSA network, NPR reports.

One more thing

What’s next for IVF

IVF has brought millions of babies into the world over the last four decades. But the process can still be slow, painful, and expensive—and far from guaranteed to work. Now, a wave of new technologies aims to change that. 

Researchers are using AI to identify promising sperm and embryos, developing robotic systems that could automate parts of the IVF process, and even exploring controversial genetic editing techniques designed to prevent inherited disease.

The technologies could make IVF more effective and accessible. But they’re also raising difficult ethical questions about how far reproductive medicine should go.

Here’s what’s next for IVF.

—Jessica Hamzelou

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ One man’s mom has made him a magnificent Monty Python and the Holy Grail quilt.
+ An origamist has folded an astonishing mechanical typewriter from a single sheet of paper.
+ The Techno-Optimism Archive is a fascinating history of hype surrounding new technologies.
+ This richly illustrated travelogue traces the curious journey of citrus from the Himalayan foothills to the heart of Sicily.

item.title: This smell startup says its AI nose is as good as a human’s
item.dc:creator: Amit Katwala
item.description: In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation…
item.content:encoded:
In a lab near Newark Airport in New Jersey, a team of around 30 experienced human sniffers are slowly working their way through every odor on Earth. Their careful notes—“nutty,” “peachy,” “marine”—are cross-referenced with a chemical analysis to create a rich set of training data for what AI startup Osmo calls the world’s first foundation model for smell. The company’s goal, says founder Alex Wiltschko, is “to give computers a sense of smell.”

“Scent molecules are really the only language most species on this planet can speak,” he says. “Most species can’t communicate with sound or visually, so it truly is Earth’s original language. And it’s incredibly powerful for us, from a memory and an emotional standpoint. You can smell something once and remember it for the rest of your life. You can smell something on the street and be pulled back to high school.”

In the last few months, Wiltschko claims, Osmo’s model has achieved “human-level olfactory intelligence.” The company’s definition of this is that the model is about as good as the average person at detecting and discriminating between smells, and about as good as a junior perfume designer at creating them. It says its technology is already being used in the fragrance industry to help brands design and manufacture new scents. Last month, the company says, Osmo’s AI model outperformed in-house perfumers at one of the world’s largest consumer goods companies. Wiltschko believes it could be deployed eventually for threat detection at airports, for example, or diagnosing diseases. 

Wiltschko spun the startup out of his work at Google Brain, the search giant’s former AI research lab, in 2023, and he is running the same playbook as AI startups in other domains: Throw a lot of data at difficult problems, and see what happens. The challenge with scent, Wiltschko says, is that there was a dearth of good data. Before Osmo, there were fewer than 200,000 human descriptions of smells in existing databases, by his count. Plus, the chemical sensor devices needed to collect data are expensive, and the fragrance industry is secretive about its work on olfactory science. 

A lot of the company’s work has been in creating its own dataset of more than 10 million human labels and 800 million “scent tokens,” which describe the exact molecules and concentrations that go into creating specific odors. Osmo uses spectrometers and other chemical sensors, running around the clock, to break down the molecular makeup of everything from fruit and flowers to pantry  staples and organs. A team of around 70 trained data labelers in the US and overseas spend their days sniffing things and writing down what they smell like, using a standardized fragrance vocabulary.

Mapping out scents in this way is throwing out some unlikely parallels. In the same way that changing the order of words can drastically influence the meaning of a sentence, rearranging scent molecules in different proportions can drastically alter the smells humans perceive. “The scent tokens that define the smell of a newborn baby have massive overlap with the scent tokens in a fresh plate of cooked spaghetti,” Wiltschko says. (Specifically Barilla brand spaghetti, he says, which perhaps raises some questions for the people at the pasta factory.)

The company also creates its own scents, using a smell-printing robot the size of a school bus that mixes ingredients according to precise formulas to make samples for Osmo’s own research and fragrances for paying customers. It can design and print scents to order based on a ChatGPT-style prompt. Wiltschko flipped open his laptop to show me how the AI model worked. He opened a text box on screen, and I asked him to generate a fragrance that smelled like a Portuguese custard tart (we were in Lisbon for Web Summit), aimed at 18- to 23-year-old men. The system spent a few minutes cogitating, then generated three options for potential scent profiles that matched the brief (creamy, coconutty, fruity) and the molecules needed to create them. If I’d continued with the ordering process, my signature L’Eau de Custard would have been ready about a week later. 

Osmo’s technology has already been used to create retail fragrances, including for giants like Procter & Gamble. The Gates Foundation, which invested $5 million when Osmo launched, later gave the company a $3.5 million grant to assess molecules that repel disease-carrying insects, and Osmo identified eight substances that were more repellent than DEET. Osmo has also worked with StockX, the online clothing marketplace, on using smell to spot counterfeit sneakers by detecting differences in the chemical composition of the materials used in the shoes.

But not everyone is convinced by the technology or the company’s big claims. Avery Gilbert, a smell scientist and author of What the Nose Knows, has been sharply critical of Osmo on his Substack, arguing that some of its marketing claims are undocumented, and that its patent filings still rely on human sensory panels and perfumers, rather than AI. “This heavy reliance on human sensory judgments seems odd for a company premised on super-cool AI,” he wrote in March. A representative for Osmo did not respond in time for publication. 

Michael Schmuker, a former professor of neural computation at the University of Hertfordshire who has previously consulted for Osmo, says the company’s technology is an achievement. With colleagues, he created an open-source, reverse-engineered version of Osmo’s 2023 model, but it lacks the reams of data the company has collected since. 

But even with all this smell data, Osmo may be missing some of the factors that make human olfaction unique, Schmuker says. “Smell is super complex. Context is very important for smell. The same molecule may evoke a different association depending on context,” he says. “[The smell of] a French cheese like Camembert is partly the same molecule as in used nappies. You don’t confuse the two because of the context.”

In a controlled setting like a fragrance lab, this lack of context may not matter so much. But it could have an impact if Osmo’s technology becomes, as Wiltschko suggests, the “olfactive channel” for AI world models. Imagine a machine that could sniff out spoilage in food on a production line, or detect tumors through smell the way dogs have been trained to do in pilot studies.

For that to happen, sensor technology will need to get a lot better, Schmuker says. The models will need to keep improving. Medical diagnostics is the biggest prize. 

“There’s a lot of history of companies that have gone directly at that mountain peak and, unfortunately, not been successful, because it is very expensive and it is very difficult,” Wiltschko says. “So what we’re doing is building this foundation at the foothills of all these mountains. We’re sending expeditions up to the mountains, doing explorations, and basically smelling the whole world.”

item.title: Hydropower hit record lows in the US Southwest this summer
item.dc:creator: Casey Crownhart
item.description: The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration. Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an…
item.content:encoded:
The US Southwest generated 28% less electricity via hydropower between April and August than the 10-year average, according to new data from the US Energy Information Administration.

Most hydropower plants in the US rely on dams to hold back water, creating reservoirs. The water can be released through turbines, generating electricity on demand. But an extreme, prolonged drought in the Colorado River Basin has resulted in dangerously low water levels in the Southwest’s two largest reservoirs, affecting the availability of this power source.

Residents and farmers in the US Southwest, a region that includes Arizona, New Mexico, and parts of Nevada and California, rely on water that melts in the spring from snowpack in the mountains and is slowly allowed to flow south via dam releases. Snowfall in the Rocky Mountains provides about 85% of the annual flow of the Colorado River. And in recent years, the river has seen record-low flows. 

Two reservoirs along the Colorado River, Lake Powell and Lake Mead, have struggled to stay above the minimum level required for hydropower plants. At the end of September, Lake Powell’s depth was 3,518 feet, less than 1% above the level required to run the water through turbines that produce electricity at the Glen Canyon power plant. The Hoover Dam power plant requires 950 feet in Lake Mead, and that reservoir was 9% above the minimum in September.

Together, the two plants produced nearly seven terawatt-hours of electricity in 2025, enough to serve over 2 million people. 

Low water levels have been an ongoing struggle for the region, which has been in a drought for 27 years. Meanwhile, climate change is continuing to shift rainfall and snowfall patterns across the region and around the world. 

The effects of climate change on hydropower aren’t entirely straightforward globally—some regions will see more rain and snow because of shifting weather patterns, while others are likely to see less. 

But it’s playing a role for hydropower availability, according to one 2022 review study. Rising temperatures bring more droughts, warmer winters means less snow and ice to fill the reservoirs, and more variability in precipitation can lead to alternating floods and droughts, making the power source less reliable. 

Hydropower production is likely to be at its lowest level in over a decade in 2026 and tick even lower in 2027, according to projections from the EIA.

El Niño could provide some temporary relief. Sometimes this weather pattern can mean cooler, wetter conditions for the southern US. Heavy rains brought floods to the region in October and early November, and the water levels in Lake Powell rose more than 20 feet from their mid-September low. But the water is still quite low, and it’ll take much more to help reservoirs recover from decades of drought conditions.

Even as a changing climate complicates the availability of hydropower, the decline in capacity could push greenhouse-gas emissions higher. In 2023, energy-related greenhouse-gas emissions rose by 1.1% globally. A worldwide shortfall in hydropower generation accounted for about 40% of that rise, according to a report from the International Energy Agency.

item.title: The Download: Jensen Huang’s open-source dilemma and cognitive immortality
item.dc:creator: Thomas Macaulay
item.description: This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology. The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back A petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO has attracted more than 115,000 signatures, including Elon Musk, but comb through the names, and…
item.content:encoded:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back

A petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as Nvidia CEO has attracted more than 115,000 signatures, including Elon Musk, but comb through the names, and you’ll notice a significant number come from a particular slice of the tech world: open-source AI.

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for open source, but his credibility as an advocate is now under threat. Revelations about Nvidia chips in China and a new rule in the US could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress

Read the full story to find out why.

—James O’Donnell

This story is from The Algorithm, our weekly AI newsletter. Sign up to receive it in your inbox every Monday.

Roundtables: inside the quest for cognitive immortality

The quest to overcome the human brain’s limits is moving beyond science fiction. From gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud, researchers and technologists are exploring radical ways to extend human cognition. Today, MIT Technology Review examines these ideas in a live Roundtables discussion.

Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado to explore what cognitive immortality could look like, and how close we might be to achieving it.

Tune in live today, Tuesday, November 17, at 5:00 p.m. GMT / 12:00 p.m. EST / 9:00 a.m. PST.

Want to join the conversation? Subscribe to MIT Technology Review for exclusive access to all our Roundtables.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 The US is tightening controls on China’s remote access to AI chips
It’s closed a loophole that let Chinese firms access US chips abroad. (AP)
+  Xi may retaliate ahead of this week’s summit with Trump. (Bloomberg $)
+ Nvidia is warning customers against renting chips to China. (CNBC)
+ China is expanding AI distillation to work around curbs. (Reuters $)
+ Nvidia privately said it can track chips to China. (MIT Technology Review)

2 US hyperscale data centers are emitting as much CO2 as Denmark
A new study found emissions tripled between 2018 and 2025. (Verge)
+ 400 data centers use more electricity than Michigan. (Wired $)
+ Nations want to harness AI to cut emissions. (Nature)
+ But AI models can quickly become climate crisis deniers. (Guardian)

3 California has sued OpenAI over rogue AI hacking incidents
The attorney general said the company failed to protect the public. (FT $)
+ And that it admitted to 80 cases of losing control of models. (CNBC)
+ Who’s liable when AI agents go rogue? (MIT Technology Review)

4 The Supreme Court has rejected Trump’s bid to cut research grants
Lower courts found the moves likely violated free speech rights. (CBS)
+ Trump has dealt heavy blows to US science. (MIT Technology Review)

5 Widespread online outages have hit major US banks
Thousands of customers reported account access problems. (Gizmodo)
+ A separate outage delayed United Airlines flights. (Reuters $)

6 Alice Huang’s husband built a data-center empire in China
He won government backing as his wife pursued Nvidia chips. (WSJ $)
+ MAGA is using the scandal to weaken Trump’s Big Tech ties. (Axios)

7 China has sacked a scientist after a child died in a gene-editing trial
The girl died after receiving an experimental therapy in 2025. (Nature)
+ Startups want new rules on gene-editing. (MIT Technology Review)

8 America’s EV boom is happening without car buyers
Delivery fleets, robotaxis, and police cars are going electric. (Atlantic $)

9 New cosmic data has challenged our model of the universe
The findings suggest dark energy may be weakening. (Quanta)

10 A Buddhist sect plans to build an AI guru for Silicon Valley
It wants to create a model based on a collective mind. (New Yorker $)

Quote of the day

“Export controls 2.0 is here.”

—Neil Shah, vice president of research at Counterpoint Research, tells Reuters that Washington has opened a new front in its campaign to slow China’s AI ambitions.

One more thing


Welcome to Kenya’s Great Carbon Valley: a bold new gamble to fight climate change

Kenya’s Great Rift Valley is home to five geothermal power stations, which harness clouds of steam to generate about a quarter of the country’s electricity. But some of the energy escapes into the atmosphere, while even more remains underground for lack of demand. That’s what brought Octavia Carbon here.

Last year, the startup began harnessing some of that excess energy to remove CO2 from the air. The company says the method is efficient, affordable, and—crucially—scalable. But the project also faces fierce opposition. 

Read the full story on the future of Kenya’s “Great Carbon Valley.”


—Diana Kruzman

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ A gorilla rescued as an orphan and rewilded has now had a baby of her own.
+ Kelowna, British Columbia, has elected a man who ran for city council as a joke.
+ A vast new data dump from the Euclid space telescope covers a stunning section of the sky and 900 million galaxies.
+ Scientists recreated the long-lost chirps of Jurassic insects to produce a soundscape from 165 million years ago.

item.title: The open-source movement wants Jensen Huang back
item.dc:creator: James O'Donnell
item.description: This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here. On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia…
item.content:encoded:
This story originally appeared in The Algorithm, our weekly newsletter on AI. To get stories like this in your inbox first, sign up here.

On Friday, a petition to reinstate Jensen Huang as CEO of Nvidia began circulating on social media, and by Monday it listed some notable signatories, including Elon Musk and several influential Nvidia researchers. But comb through the more than 115,000 names and you’ll notice a significant faction of Huang’s supporters—higher-ups from Hugging Face, a hub for sharing AI models, and venture capital firms Andreessen Horowitz and Sequoia Capital—come from a particular slice of the tech world.

These names have a vested interest in the development of open-source AI, models that, unlike ChatGPT or Claude, can be downloaded and run independent of large tech companies. Supporters of such models say that concentrating AI in the hands of a few powerful companies will leave everyone else worse off (a concern that wouldn’t sound out of place among the AI industry’s critics on the left, if so many open-source advocates weren’t also venture capitalists who stand to profit when startups can build on cheaper AI without paying Big Tech).

Huang had become a sort of ringleader for those who defend open source to policymakers against concerns that such models come with no guardrails and cede AI leadership to China, where the most powerful and popular open-source models are created. They now want their most influential voice returned to his post. 

But it’s not just Huang’s extramarital affairs that threaten his (and Nvidia’s) credibility as an advocate for open-source AI. New research into China’s startups using Nvidia’s chips, and a new rule from the US Department of Commerce announced Monday, could deal a blow to both the movement’s reputation and its technical progress. 

On Thursday, the day Huang resigned, ex-OpenAI researcher Will DePue published findings online suggesting that China’s AI companies had far more access to Nvidia’s advanced Blackwell chips than previously estimated. China is banned from accessing Nvidia’s most cutting-edge chips to help protect America’s AI lead.

It’s unclear how they would have gained access to the chips. DePue claims the results were verified by senior researchers at OpenAI and Anthropic, but an independent analysis has not confirmed the results. (DePue did not respond to a request for an interview. Nvidia did not immediately respond to a request for comment.)

The findings do not establish that Nvidia helped Chinese companies obtain the chips, and the broader problem of chip smuggling was already known to extend well beyond Nvidia’s control.

But in suggesting that Nvidia may have profited from the rise of Chinese AI startups, whose models are increasingly being used by American companies instead of domestic alternatives, the findings do leave Huang in an awkward position. He has championed open-source AI as a way to strengthen American technological leadership. “Without open source, startups can’t thrive, university researchers can’t do research, you can’t teach AI, scientists can’t use AI,” he said last December during a talk about helping the US win the AI race against China.

It also makes the idea of reinstating Huang even more of a long shot. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent even said last week that Nvidia should not consider someone from inside the company to replace him. The new findings lower Huang’s chances further.

What happens next? Nvidia announced in September it would acquire Hugging Face for nearly $13 billion. Its support for open source also serves a straightforward financial interest: The more businesses that build their own models instead of forking over money to Anthropic and OpenAI, the more chips Nvidia can sell. 

But a new rule from the US Department of Commerce could mean the models popular on Hugging Face will soon stop getting smarter. The rule aims to prevent Chinese companies from training models on Nvidia chips that they can’t own directly, but that they can access remotely in data centers in countries like Malaysia—a workaround that has helped China’s open-source models get so good.

The open-source world rallied around Huang because of his influence on policymakers. That was important, since the rise of China’s open-source models has splintered some in Trump’s orbit. If Huang is out, who is next?

item.title: Building trustworthy AI by fencing it in, not predicting it
item.dc:creator: Sudhi Sinha
item.description: In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do…
item.content:encoded:
In October this year, OpenAI disclosed that two of its AI agents had switched off the systems built to monitor them. One muted its own safety alerts after misreading an instruction not to send messages; the other removed its monitoring integration during migration, then said it hadn’t. No rule had told the agents to do that, and no test had anticipated the behaviors.

For a century, we have built trust in technology on predictability: predefined inputs, predictable outputs, and layers of protection. Consider how a breaker trips at a set current or an aircraft component is tested against known (i.e., predictable) stresses.

AI changes that. Traditional software executes instructions written by humans, whereas AI exercises what might be called synthetic judgment. We use AI because it can interpret situations we did not program and generate responses we did not prescribe. But the more freedom we give AI, the harder it becomes to provide the predictability on which trust has traditionally been built.

We will not make AI trustworthy by predicting what it will do. We will do it by fencing it in with hard limits that are enforced outside its reach. In OpenAI’s case, the safeguards sat inside a system the agents could edit. But a fence the agents can simply move is not a fence.

Where traditional definitions of trust fall short

Recent MIT Technology Review coverage has approached this problem from other directions. One contributor argues that having a human in the loop is an insufficient solution because humans are fundamentally unable to understand AI systems’ intentions and advocates instead for interdisciplinary research and collaboration between academia, government, and the tech industry. And a story on reverse game theory describes using incentives to keep models from deviating from the rules, even when no one understands how they work on the inside.

Both articles acknowledge that we cannot understand or watch every AI decision. Our instruments of trust, including requirements, testing, certification, safety margins, interlocks, and pass/fail criteria, all depend on our ability to bound a system’s behavior. This is the determinism paradox.

With generative and agentic AI, behavior is shaped by training data, architecture, prompts, context, retrieval sources, and the environment. Inputs change, models are updated, tools change, and agents interact. Small variations propagate into outcomes nobody designed. The problem is not randomness; it is that the space of possible behavior is too large to enumerate in advance. Trust must therefore be engineered around boundaries rather than predicted outputs. The goal is not deterministic AI, but bounded, observable, and controllable AI. Trust also cannot be a one-time test. Traditional assurance certifies a product at a point in time, but AI keeps evolving after deployment, and a system that has passed every test can drift outside the conditions that made those tests meaningful. Trust must be continuously earned.

Safety engineering has been accounting for some of this variability for decades. For example, the Nuclear Regulatory Commission determine the likelihood of failures in complex systems, and Systems-Theoretic Accident Model and Processes (STAMP) showed that accidents can emerge from interactions among working components, people, and organizations. But AI raises the stakes, because just a single component can now interpret, infer, and act. The stakes rise further as AI moves from browsers into vehicles, robots, medical systems, industrial controls, and data centers, where a wrong answer can become a life-threatening event.

Building trust that scales

It’s clear that a person rubber-stamping thousands of AI actions an hour is not an acceptable—or scalable—safeguard against risk. But the remedy is not to remove people from the loop; it is to put human judgment where it counts: setting limits in advance and approving the rare actions that have serious consequences while hard constraints handle the rest.

Therefore, trust has to move upstream into architecture. The central questions become: What authority are we willing to give AI, under what conditions, and supported by what evidence? And what happens outside those conditions? That is very different from asking whether a model scored 94% on a benchmark.

The determinism paradox does not mean AI cannot be trusted. It means trust needs a different architecture. Instead of making every output predictable, make the boundaries predictable. An AI medical assistant may be probabilistic in its diagnosis, but deterministic rules govern whether it can change a prescription. An industrial AI may find many ways to optimize a process, while fixed limits keep it within pressure and temperature bounds. An agent may decide how to complete a task, while permissions, transaction limits, and human approvals determine what it is authorized to do.

Let AI be probabilistic inside the box and make the box itself deterministic wherever consequences matter. Leaders can put this into practice by asking five questions:

  1. What authority does AI have? Define not only what it can do but what it is allowed to do, separating interpretation, recommendation, decision, and execution.
  2. Is the function of AI proportional to the consequence? A marketing copilot and AI controlling industrial equipment need different assurance thresholds.
  3. Are we taking the appropriate steps toward autonomy? For example, there needs to be a plan to move from having AI interpret while humans decide, to AI making recommendations, to then taking action with approval, and ultimately to having supervised autonomy, but only as AI can safely work at each step.
  4. Are we testing the system or merely the model? Unexpected interactions emerge among models, data, agents, APIs, and human workflows.
  5. Are we continuously earning trust? Monitor drift, failures, near-misses, and model changes throughout the lifecycle.

The winners in AI will be those who solve the determinism paradox—giving AI enough freedom to create value while engineering boundaries strong enough to make what it does with that freedom trustworthy. Invention earns attention. Trust earns adoption.

item.content:encoded:
This is today’s edition of The Download, our weekday newsletter that provides a daily dose of what’s going on in the world of technology.

Are we there yet? Six technologies that promised to change the world

How do you measure progress towards the future? In the Impossible issue of MIT Technology Review, our series “Are we there yet?” examines how far six potentially transformative technologies have come after years of promises.

We spoke to experts, researchers and engineers to find out what’s holding them back, then scored each on a progress meter from zero to ten.  Find out how we rated each of these technologies—and how close they are to delivering on their promise.

Nuclear-powered spaceships
Exercise in a pill
Interspecies communication
Solid-state batteries
Cleaning up PFAS
Eliminating traffic deaths

Subscribe now to get every issue of our print magazine as soon as it lands.

Inside the quest for cognitive immortality

Could technology keep your brain going beyond death? Far-thinking technologists are exploring ways to make it happen, from gradual brain replacement to uploading memories to the cloud. MIT Technology Review’s latest Roundtables event explores these ideas and how close they might be to reality.

Join science editor Mary Beth Griggs and senior editor for biomedicine Antonio Regalado for this subscriber-only discussion tomorrow.

Tune in live on Tuesday, November 17 at 5:00 p.m. GMT / 12:00 p.m. EST / 9:00 a.m. PST.

The must-reads

I’ve combed the internet to find you today’s most fun/important/scary/fascinating stories about technology.

1 Jensen Huang is considering a comeback as Nvidia CEO
He’s discussed with confidants the possibility of returning. (FT $)
+ Elon Musk has joined 165,000 signatories calling for his recall. (Guardian)
+ The Treasury Secretary wants them to hire an outsider. (Axios)
+ ​​Megaspeed says the alleged China spy left the company last year. (BBC)
+ Trump plans to name Nvidia an AI “national champion.” (WSJ $)
+ Nvidia privately said it can track chips to China. (MIT Technology Review)

2 SpaceX has caught a rocket returning from orbit for the first time
The feat brings fully reusable rockets closer to reality. (Guardian)
+ The feat shows what audacious engineering can achieve. (Atlantic $)
+ Meanwhile, Ukraine says SpaceX is lying about Starshield speed restrictions. (Reuters $)

3 The US and allies have agreed to guard AI supply chains from China
Ten countries will collaborate to secure critical technologies. (FT $)
+ Chinese AI stocks have plunged on export control fears. (Information $)
+ Nvidia privately said it can track chips to China. (MIT Technology Review)

4 The US flight shutdown exposed weaknesses in air traffic technology
Officials blamed the disruption on a faulty router installation. (Reuters $)
+ It was a terrible week of outages. (WP $)

5 The first in-body CRISPR treatment is set to reach patients next year
The treatment could gain FDA approval as early as March. (Nature)
+ CRISPR has created female clones of male mice. (MIT Technology Review)

6 Congress plans to make data centers pay billions more for power
A proposed bill would shift grid costs onto tech companies. (NYT $)
+ Utilities also want tech giants to pay more for power. (Bloomberg $)
+ Is data center hatred all about electricity? (MIT Technology Review)

7 Apple plans to launch its first smart glasses next year
It’s betting on Siri to give the specs an edge. (Verge)

8 Bill Gates has made billions from climate-polluting landfills
His investment in a landfill operator is worth $29 billion. (ProPublica)

9 ​​A new AI device turns everyday objects into needy virtual pets
The tiny gadgets aim to encourage healthier everyday habits. (Wired $)

10 Scientists made monkeys watch Minions to study their brains
Their findings challenge traditional vision models. (404 Media)

Quote of the day

“If our hopes for the future are pinned on any one individual being trustworthy, then we’re pretty screwed.”

—Helen Toner, former OpenAI board member, tells The Verge that AI needs stronger governance than trusting tech executives to do the right thing.

One more thing


How AI and Wikipedia have sent vulnerable languages into a doom spiral

When Kenneth Wehr started managing the Greenlandic-language version of Wikipedia, he discovered that almost every article had been written by people who didn’t speak the language. 

A growing number of them had been copy-pasted into Wikipedia from machine translators—and were riddled with elementary mistakes. This is beginning to cause a wicked problem.

AI systems, from Google Translate to ChatGPT, learn new languages by scraping text from Wikipedia. This could push the most vulnerable languages on Earth toward the precipice.

Read the full story on what happens when AI gets trained on junk pages.


—Jacob Judah

We can still have nice things

A place for comfort, fun, and distraction to brighten up your day. (Got any ideas? Drop me a line.)

+ Adelaide Zoo is celebrating its first cassowary eggs in 34 years.
+ Photos fill the frame at the Epson Pano awards, which celebrate panoramic photography.
+ Indonesia has called an early halt to the world’s largest deforestation project, saving up to 4 million acres.
+ After over a month on the loose in Yellowstone, a little dog called Luna has been reunited with her owners.
